To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) expression of pea lectin (PSl) or wild soybean lectin-nucleotid phosphohydrolas (GS52) genes in transgenic rice promoted root colonization by Rhizobium spp. and 2) the PSL or GS52 lectins in transgenic rice were targeted to root hair tips and promoted localized root cell dissolution by compatible rhizobial strains.
the legume symbiosis genes psl and g52 promote rhizobial root colonization in rice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of transgenic plants with improved nitrogen fixing capacity.
the development of transgenic rice plants expressing the pea and wild soybean lectin genes.
the development of transgenic rice plants that can be used as a source of nitrogen for the rice plants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the expression of the legume lectins PSL (in pea) and GS52 (in soybean) promotes bacterial colonization of the root epidermal/ root hair cells of rice and that this occurs through a process of bacterial attachment and subsequent cell wall dissolution at the root hair tips.

lectins, which participate in recognition of compatible rhizobial strains by root epidermis in legume hosts, are also able not only to facilitate rhizobia colonization of root epidemal cells, but also to promote the formation of root nodules in transgenic rice plants.

the expression of the pea lectin PSL and the wild-soybean lectin GS52 in the root epidermal cell layers of transgenic rice plants significantly promoted colonization of root epidersis cells by the rhizobia, and the bacterial colonization was preferentially at the root hair tips of the rice plants.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
lectin genes from pea and soybean were expressed in rice and that this expression promoted rhizobium colonization of rice roots.

we were able to show that the lectins, PSL and GS-52, which play a crucial role in recognition and attachment of the compatible Rhizobia in legumes, are also able, when expressed in rice, to promote rhizobial root colonization in this cereal crop, and that they also target the root hair tip region, as is the case with legumes, to facilitate bacterial attachment/colonizations.
we were able to show that expression of the lectin gene in rice promotes rhizobium attachment/colonization of rice roots.
The main takeaway from our work is that

lectins, such that PSL and GS 52, are able to facilitate rhizo-bial colonization of rice roots, and that this is likely to be due to the ability of these lectins to promote localized cell wall dissolution at the root hair tips by compatible rhizobial hydrolytic activity.
lectins are able to promote rhizobial infection in non-legume plants, and that this is due to their ability to promote the dissolution of root cell walls.
lectins, which are involved in rhizobium recognition and attachment to the roots of legumes, are also able, when expressed in rice, to promote rhizobial root colonization in this non-legume plant.
